archetype.name: Rebuilding
archetype.definition: A team coming off a last-place finish that is again last on the site and is being outplayed so badly at 5-on-5 that the standings are the least of its worries.

report.headline: Last on the ice and on the sheet, and the finishing is propping it up
report.take:
Vancouver is 2-10-1, 32nd of 32 on the site, and it has earned that ranking. Last season ended 25-49-8 with 58 points and a last-place site rank, and nothing in the first month suggests a turn. The Canucks own the league's worst Goal Diff / GP at -1.77, the worst defense by goals against, and a 0-9-1 run over their last 10 that includes a 10-game losing streak. They won in September and won once in October.

The root cause is territory. Vancouver's 5-on-5 xGF % of 37.1% and CF % of 41% are bottom-two marks, and the raw shot counts are worse: 19.8 shots a game for, last in the league, against 33.5 allowed, also last. That is 7.6 shots a game below the league average and 6.6 above it the other way. Last season's xGF % was 44.2%, already poor, so this is a step backward. When a team gets outshot like that, the forwards grade out D-, the blueline D-, and the defense gives up the most winger production in the league.

Two things in the numbers mislead in opposite directions. Skater shooting is 14.3%, third-best in the league and three points above average. That is the only reason a team with the fewest shots sits 22nd in goals rather than last, and it will not hold. The other is luck. Pts vs Goal Diff of -3.6 is the league's worst, and the last 10 include one-goal losses to Vegas, the Islanders and Florida in overtime. The goaltending F is mostly one man: Kevin Lankinen's .812 save % and -12.1 GSAx sit last on the goalie tab, while Leevi Merilainen's .912 and +3.7 rank 19th of 69.

Where it goes from here depends on who plays goal and whether the penalty kill, at 64.4%, stops being a disaster. Better luck in close games and more Merilainen starts should lift the 32-point pace. Cooling finishing will push the other way. The likeliest result is a team that is less embarrassing than this pace but still at or near the bottom of the league.

strengths.title: Merilainen is a real NHL goalie
strengths.body: Across six starts Merilainen has a .912 save % and 3.7 GSAx, 19th of 69 on the goalie tab, behind a defense that gives up the most shots in the league. The team's .867 save % is almost entirely Lankinen's doing. Save % in six starts is a thin sample, but it is the one piece of the roster performing above average, and leaning on it is the clearest path to more points.

strengths.title: A power play that functions
strengths.body: At 21.6% the power play ranks 14th and sits just above the league average of 21.2%, the only special-teams or territorial number that isn't bottom-tier. Elias Pettersson, the center, drives it: 13 points with 6 on the power play, matched by Brock Boeser's 6 PP points. Because it relies on a few skilled players rather than on territory, it is the most sustainable part of the offense.

strengths.title: Pettersson on the blueline holds up
strengths.body: Elias Pettersson, the defenseman, ranks 19th of 250 on the defense tab. He has the best xGF % among the defensemen at 43.9% and a +3 rating on a team that is losing almost every night. He is the one bright spot on a blueline graded D-, though the 25-minute workload goes to Filip Hronek.

concerns.title: Buried at 5-on-5
concerns.body: An xGF % of 37.1% and a CF % of 41% mean Vancouver spends most of its even-strength time defending. The shot gap of 19.8 for against 33.5 allowed is the worst in the league at both ends. Every regular forward is under 41% in expected-goal share, so no single line is to blame. That matches a roster without enough puck-movers, and it gives little reason to expect a quick fix.

concerns.title: A penalty kill that isn't killing
concerns.body: The PK at 64.4% is last and 13.9 points below the league average. When the team's worst goalie by a mile is in net for half the starts, short-handed time turns into goals against. Some recovery toward last season's 71.5% is likely. Even that would still be poor, and it remained a bottom-tier kill throughout the previous season.

concerns.title: Scoring rides unsustainable finishing
concerns.body: Skaters are converting 14.3% of their shots, third in the league and three points above the 11.3% average. On the league's lowest shot volume, that hot finishing is what keeps the offense 22nd rather than last. When it cools toward normal, the offense will slide unless the shot counts rise, and the shot counts are the worst in hockey.

trend.note: A win in the September opener and one more early gave way to a 0-9-1 run over the last 10 and a 10-game losing streak. The last five were marginally less lopsided, but points have nearly stopped coming.

weekAhead.headline: Two beatable Pacific road games, then Toronto
weekAhead.body:
This is as soft a stretch as a last-place team gets. Two road games against division sides in the bottom third of the site come first: Anaheim is 25th and San Jose 21st. Both also lose the territorial battle, with Anaheim at a 44% xGF % and San Jose at 41.7%, so Vancouver should not be chasing the puck quite as hopelessly. Anaheim's defense ranks 30th against wingers, an opening for a team whose wing scoring runs through Boeser, Lekkerimaki and DeBrusk.

San Jose is the trickier of the two because of special teams and goaltending. The Sharks' power play is sixth at 26.8% and meets the league's worst kill, and their goaltending is graded A- with 6.3 GSAx. Toronto at home on Saturday is the hard one: sixth on the site with an A- forward group and the league's best penalty kill at 95.2%. That kill neutralizes the one Vancouver unit that works. Realistically the week is about breaking the streak against Anaheim or San Jose.

keyMatchups.title: Canucks PK vs Sharks power play
keyMatchups.body: San Jose converts 26.8% of its power plays, sixth in the league, and Vancouver kills just 64.4%, last. Staying out of the box matters more in this game than any other this week.

keyMatchups.title: Vancouver wingers vs Anaheim's defense
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim allows the third-most winger production relative to expectation, ranking 30th. With Lekkerimaki and DeBrusk among Vancouver's better-ranked forwards, Monday is the best chance for the offense to get going without depending on hot shooting.

keyMatchups.title: Vancouver PP vs Toronto's kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's penalty kill is first at 95.2%, which blunts Vancouver's only league-average unit. Five-on-five, Toronto's A- forwards face a defense that has allowed the most forward production in the league.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal: Merilainen's .912 against Lankinen's .812 is the difference between competitive losses and blowouts.

restOfSeason.body:
The 32-point pace overstates how bad the record will finish. A Pts vs Goal Diff of -3.6 in one-goal games tends to even out, and giving Merilainen most of the starts would cut the goals against noticeably. Working the other way, the 14.3% shooting that props up the offense should fade toward the league's 11.3%. Unless the shot counts rise from the league's lowest, goals for will drop to compensate. The 5-on-5 numbers are worse than last season's, when this team won 25 games, so matching that would count as progress.

Expect a final total somewhere around 20 to 27 wins and roughly 48 to 62 standings points, still in the league's bottom tier. Goals against should settle near 3.8 to 4.3 a game as the kill and goaltending recover partway. Scoring will likely drift down toward roughly 2.4 to 2.8 a game.

confidence.note: Only 13 games, but the shot and expected-goal gaps are extreme and match last season's last-place profile.
